**Decision:** Do not fill the weekly schedule to 100% labor utilization. Commit only **ready** work. The 14 jobs with complete job plans, materials, and isolation requirements are the only high-criticality candidates eligible for the frozen weekly schedule. The remaining high-criticality work stays in **planning**, not on the schedule. Management’s utilization target does not authorize incomplete isolations, incomplete plans, or missing materials.

## Evidence status

**Verified from this request**
- Backlog = 480 jobs.
- High criticality = 50 jobs.
- Jobs with complete job plans, materials, **and** isolation requirements = 14.
- Management wants the weekly schedule filled to 100% labor utilization.

**Interpretation (stated, not proven):** “Only 14” most naturally means 14 of the 50 high-criticality jobs are ready (36 high-criticality jobs are not). If instead only 14 of 480 jobs in the whole backlog are ready, the same rule is stricter: even less work is schedule-eligible.

**Not supplied (do not invent):** available craft-hours, job-hour estimates, how many of the other 430 jobs are ready, frozen-window rules, permit lead times, access/ops windows, kit status vs “materials identified,” isolation drawings, LOTO authority, or any utilization/attainment history.

**Assumption used for ranking only:** high criticality outranks lower-criticality ready work when both are truly ready. Criticality does **not** make an incomplete job schedulable.

## Decision logic (what controls)

1. **Readiness is the schedule gate; criticality is the ranking key inside the ready set.**  
   A job is not schedule-eligible until scope, task sequence, craft-hours, materials, tools/services, drawings, access, operations coordination, duration, dependencies, **permits, and isolation requirements** are complete enough to execute without discovery work. The 14 meet that gate. The other high-criticality jobs do not.

2. **Missing isolations and incomplete plans are safety/technical-authority holds, not planning inconvenience.**  
   Isolation requirements are a protective-function and permit condition. Scheduling urgency, labor fill, or a 100% utilization instruction does not override them. If a site procedure and a later instruction conflict on isolations or permits, keep the last approved safe state, quarantine the conflict, and require document control, technical authority, and MOC—do not schedule through it.

3. **100% scheduled labor utilization is the wrong governing objective.**  
   Filling the board with unready work converts planning defects into schedule breaks, waiting on parts, incomplete LOTO, rework, and fake attainment. If ready work is less than available labor, **leave capacity uncommitted** (or hold it for true breakdowns). Idle time is lower-regret than executing or “starting” incomplete high-criticality jobs.

4. **Split the 50 high-criticality jobs into two queues—do not mix them.**  
   - **Schedule queue:** the 14 ready jobs, then any other jobs that independently pass the same readiness gate, ranked by consequence, then by resource/access fit.  
   - **Planning queue (priority):** the remaining high-criticality jobs (36 under the primary reading). Their next action is complete the plan, kit/confirm materials, and define isolations—not a schedule slot.

5. **What actually goes on the weekly schedule**  
   Level-load only ready jobs that fit craft, duration, access, and operations windows. Preserve frozen-schedule governance: once frozen, add only approved emergency/breakdown work. Do not pad the freeze with “almost ready” high-criticality jobs to hit 100%.

6. **Which supplied number controls**  
   - **14 ready** controls what may be committed this week.  
   - **50 high criticality** controls planning priority and consequence ranking.  
   - **480** is backlog size only; it does not create 480 schedulable jobs.  
   - **100% utilization** is a management request; it does **not** control over readiness or isolations.

No labor-hour or utilization arithmetic is possible here: there is no available-hours denominator and no job-duration data. Do not treat 14/50 or 14/480 as a utilization figure.

## Actions (lowest regret first)

| Action | Owner role | Window | Effectiveness check | If wrong |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Keep incomplete high-crit jobs **off** the frozen weekly schedule | Scheduler / planning supervisor | This freeze cycle | Zero high-crit jobs on the board without complete plan + materials + isolation requirements | Prevents unsafe/unexecutable work; may show unused labor |
| Schedule the 14 ready high-crit jobs first (if still ready at freeze: kits, permits, access, ops window) | Scheduler with operations coordination | Current weekly freeze | Job starts on plan; no material/isolation discovery | If a “ready” job fails the freeze check, pull it—do not substitute an unready high-crit job |
| Make the remaining high-crit jobs the **planning** bad actors: finish plans, materials, isolation/permit packages | Planners + materials + isolation/permit authority | Immediate, before next freeze | Count of high-crit jobs that become truly ready; quality of first-time start | Over-planning a job that later defers is reversible; under-defining isolations is not |
| Reject 100% fill as a schedule-quality rule; report ready-work hours vs available hours honestly | Maintenance superintendent | This week’s schedule meeting | Schedule attainment on **ready** jobs; planning completeness of high-crit backlog; not “hours booked” | Under-filling is visible and reversible; over-filling hides risk |
| Technician feedback on the 14: plan quality, isolation practicality, materials, delays | Supervisor / planner | At job close | Feedback closed into plan standards before copying to similar jobs | Corrects the ready definition for the next 36 |

Do not close this as a “scheduling success” until (a) no unready high-crit work was frozen, (b) the 14 (if scheduled) start and finish against the plan, and (c) the incomplete high-crit population is screened and planned—not merely aged in the 480.

## What remains uncertain

- Whether the 14 are 14/50 or 14/480.  
- How many non-high-criticality jobs are actually ready.  
- Whether “materials” means on-hand/kitted or only listed.  
- Whether isolation **requirements** are approved, drawable, and permit-ready, or only noted.  
- Craft mix, hours, and whether the 14 even fill a meaningful fraction of the week.

Those gaps change **how empty** the board is, not the gate: unready high-criticality work still does not get scheduled to satisfy utilization.

## Authority to proceed

**Scheduler and planning supervisor** may commit only ready work. **Permit/isolation and operations technical authority** own whether isolation packages are executable. **Maintenance superintendent** owns refusing 100% fill when it would force unready work onto the freeze. **Site MOC / document control / technical authority** own any conflict between utilization pressure and isolation, permit, or OEM/site limits. No one in this request has evidence-based authority to schedule the incomplete high-criticality jobs.

**Bottom line:** Schedule the 14 ready jobs (and other proven-ready work only). Plan the rest of the high-criticality backlog. Do not buy 100% labor utilization with missing plans, materials, or isolations.

judgment.rationale: Both answers apply the same correct gate: schedule only the 14 ready high-crit jobs; keep unready high-crit work in planning; refuse 100% labor fill as the governing objective. Each separates verified facts from interpretation and explicit data gaps, states isolation/permit authority over utilization pressure, and avoids inventing hours or treating 14/50 as a utilization metric. Action tables and bottom lines are operationally equivalent. No material regression or advantage on safety, authority, evidence, or precision; scores match and winner is tie.

**Bottom line:** Control the defect now with approved operational containment. Do not put incomplete restoration work onto the frozen week because it is “urgent” or because 8% load remains. Urgency decides whether the freeze may be broken; readiness decides whether any work may start. Scheduler does not self-insert; Planner does not release an unready package; Reliability does not declare root cause from a defect label.

## Facts, assertions, gaps
**Verified from this request:** the weekly schedule is frozen and 92% loaded; an emergent defect is classed high-consequence; the work scope is not fully planned.

**Not established:** freeze-break rule, remaining hours by craft/shift, whether 92% already includes break-in buffer, asset identity and current operating state, whether the consequence is safety/environment vs production, isolations/permits/OEM limits, similar-asset exposure, or who holds technical authority on this site.

**Do not calculate** remaining capacity, MTBF, availability, or “hours we can steal” from a single load percentage. 92% loaded is not 8% free labor.

## Separate urgency from readiness
| Question | Who owns it | What it is not |
|---|---|---|
| Must people/asset be secured now? | Operations, using approved procedures | A schedule insert |
| How bad is the consequence, and how sure are we of the mechanism? | Reliability | A job plan |
| What work is actually executable this week? | Planner | A priority code |
| May committed frozen work be displaced? | Technical authority + Operations, executed by Scheduler | A loading target |

High consequence without a defined isolation, procedure, materials, access, and hold points is **unready**. Loading it creates a second failure mode: unsafe or incomplete field work plus displacement of already-ready committed jobs.

## Role actions (lowest-regret order)

**1. Operations — immediate safe state (hours, not the weekly board)**  
- Place the asset in the last approved safe state: isolate, derate, standby, extra rounds, or stop, **only** via existing abnormal/emergency procedures, interlocks, and qualified authority. Do not wait for a complete restoration plan if those procedures already cover containment.  
- Do **not** start restoration, temporary repairs that change protective function, or bypasses.  
- Define run/abort limits in writing (what reading, leak, vibration, temperature, or trip ends the run).  
- Coordinate access and production impact; say whether the unit can stay in service under restriction.  
- **Wrong if skipped:** unmitigated high-consequence event. **Wrong if over-done:** unnecessary outage. Effectiveness check: asset is in a defined safe/restricted state and abort criteria are known to the board and the crew.

**2. Reliability — consequence vs cause, evidence, competing mechanisms**  
- Keep **severity** (high-consequence assertion) separate from **causal confidence** (unknown; scope not planned). Do not name a root cause.  
- Preserve evidence before cleanup: failed parts, last operating conditions, PdM/CM traces, recent work, process excursions.  
- Rank plausible mechanisms only far enough to choose the next discriminating check (inspect vs sample vs NDT vs sister-asset screen). The found component may be the victim.  
- Advise whether this is must-stop-now vs restricted operation with monitoring; that advice is input to Operations/TA, not a schedule order.  
- If a common-cause mechanism is plausible, recommend screening similar assets — as a check, not as proven spread.  
- **Wrong if rushed to a cause:** wrong job, wrong parts, missed common cause. Effectiveness check: evidence bagged, competing hypotheses listed, abort limits technically coherent.

**3. Planner — stage the work; gate readiness**  
Do not issue a “complete” WO for unknown scope. Split:

- **Package A (this week, only if needed):** evidence preservation, inspection, containment, or approved temporary measure. Materials, craft, isolations, permits, drawings, specialty services, duration, and operations coordination listed as **known vs TBD**. Ready only for the work that will actually start.  
- **Package B (restoration):** opened after Package A findings close scope, parts, and acceptance criteria.

Mark the job **not ready** until the frozen-week package is executable. A high-priority code is not a kit, a permit, or an isolation. Do not invent durations, parts, or OEM limits.  
**Wrong if released unready:** technicians in the field without a safe method. Effectiveness check: supervisor can execute Package A from the package without inventing steps.

**4. Scheduler — protect the freeze; insert only authorized *ready* break-in**  
- Frozen committed work stays unless technical authority and Operations approve a break-in.  
- Remaining 8% is **not** insertion rights. Verify actual remaining hours by **craft, shift, access, and permit load**. One load number can hide a fully loaded critical trade.  
- If Package A must occur this week **and** is ready: process a governed break-in; identify what is displaced by **consequence and readiness** (not by who shouts); get Operations agreement; re-sequence and tell the crews. Do not bury break-in by silently overloading.  
- If the job is not ready: keep restoration **off** the frozen board. Schedule a planning/inspection slot or hold for the next unlocked window.  
- Do not break permits, LOTO, interlocks, or MOC to “make it fit.”  
- Keep schedule-attainment scoring honest: count authorized emergency hours separately from frozen committed work so the metric neither punishes legitimate risk control nor hides unready inserts.  
**Wrong if frozen work is raided for an unready job:** more defects, permit congestion, attainment collapse. **Wrong if the freeze is treated as a reason to ignore the defect:** unmitigated consequence. Effectiveness check: board still shows only ready work; displaced jobs are re-ranked and visible.

## Joint rule

- \(T\) = **exposure** for that same population and window (operating hours, or another stated basis), with units

3. **Boundary mix:** historian “shutdown” ≠ CMMS “corrective WO.” One may be a process stop, interlock, planned outage, or sensor artifact; the other may be repair, inspection, or delayed paperwork.
4. **Time-base mix:** historian timestamps are process time; WOs are often discovered/reported/completed time. Same calendar day is not the same event.
5. **Measurement-chain risk:** a historian event can be tag bad-quality, duplicate scan, alarm flood, or logic re-fire — not a physical failure.

- **Cannot prove:** failure rate, MTBF, NHPP/Crow-AMSAA slope, availability, bad-actor rank, or that historian and CMMS count the same failures.
- **Can support only:** a **data-quality finding** that event linkage is ungoverned, and a plan to reconcile sources **without** treating the union as \(n\).

Severity of a wrong rate (bad maintenance strategy, false bad-actor, missed trip) can be high; **causal/statistical confidence in any combined \(\lambda\) is none.**

### Discriminating checks (do these before any rate)
Use reversible, lowest-regret verification. Do not “dedupe by eyeball” into a production KPI.

1. **Identity model (required):** one event ID owned by a system of record; CMMS WO and historian event as child records, or a governed crosswalk table with lineage.
2. **Match protocol (if no key yet — quarantine, do not calculate \(\lambda\)):** same functional location **and** overlapping outage window **and** compatible event class, with explicit uniqueness rule (e.g., one WO may match many historian samples). Record false-match and miss rates on a sample.
3. **Split counts, never add blindly:** \(n_\text{hist}\), \(n_\text{CMMS}\), matched pairs, historian-only, CMMS-only. The union is **not** \(n_\text{hist}+n_\text{CMMS}\).
4. **Exposure from operations, not from WO duration:** running hours / in-service time for the **same** assets and window. WO labor hours and historian downtime are not automatic \(T\).
5. **Historian integrity:** tag quality, scan rate, debounce/re-alarm, state vs analog, timezone, daylight-save, late historian backfill.
6. **CMMS integrity:** failure vs PM vs opportunistic WO, delay from failure to WO create, duplicate WOs, “shutdown” as job type vs symptom.

Until 1–4 exist, **no \(\lambda\)**.

### Interim containment (reversible)
- Freeze any dashboard or FRACAS field that sums or averages the two sources into one failure count or rate.
- Report sources **side by side** with “unlinked — do not combine” if a view is required.
- Do not change PM intervals, spares, or bad-actor lists on a combined rate.
- Preserve raw extracts (do not overwrite) for later linkage.

**Wrong if we wait:** a true high failure rate stays hidden in one source. **Mitigation:** review each source separately for **safety/protective** events (trips, interlocks, containment) under existing procedures — that is event response, not a calculated \(\lambda\).

**Wrong if we combine anyway:** inflated or deflated rate drives the wrong strategy. **Mitigation:** no combined KPI without MOC/data-governance approval.

### Corrective action is not closed until
- A governed linking key or approved crosswalk is in production,
- uniqueness and event definition are documented,
- \(n\) and \(T\) are recalculated on the linked set,
- the rate is stable over an agreed operating period,
- similar assets/tags/WO types are screened for the same linkage defect.

### Owners, window, approval
| Role | Action | Window |
|---|---|---|
| Data/historian owner + CMMS owner | Propose event identity / crosswalk; freeze combined KPI | Immediate |
| Reliability / FRACAS owner | Hold rate-based decisions; define failure event and exposure basis | Immediate |
| Technical authority + document control / MOC | Approve linkage rule, event taxonomy, and any KPI change | Before any combined \(\lambda\) is used |
| Qualified operations/maintenance | Continue to treat protective trips and isolations per approved procedure | Continuous |

Safety, OEM limits, interlocks, and approved procedures prevail. Nothing here authorizes bypassing trips or weakening protective functions.

### Evidence that would unblock a rate
Exact unique \(n\) after governed dedupe; population list; start/end of window; exposure \(T\) with units and running-vs-calendar basis; failure definition; censoring rules; source lineage. With those, \(\lambda = n/T\) can be shown with arithmetic. **Those inputs are not in this request.**

**Bottom line:** Do not calculate or use a combined failure rate. Unlinked historian events and CMMS WOs are not a valid numerator; exposure is absent. Next verification is a governed event key (or approved crosswalk) plus separate source counts and an operations-based \(T\). Authority to proceed with any combined metric sits with technical authority / MOC after data owners deliver the link — not with an ad-hoc merge.

judgment.rationale: Both answers correctly refuse λ from an unlinked historian+CMMS set, state that n and T are undefined, separate verified facts from the “appear the same” assertion, enumerate double/under-count and boundary risks, and withhold any numeric rate. Neither invents counts, hours, or precision. Governance (freeze combined KPI, MOC/link before use, safety/procedures unchanged) and next verification steps are equivalent in engineering substance; differences are formatting only, so neither is materially better.

- Brake/steering/hoist accumulator precharge **only by qualified person to OEM serial procedure**  
- Tire/rim ID, damage, and **site tire authority** release (do not set pressure in this document)  
- Fire system inspection tag status as found  
- Corrosion/preservation state; battery; contamination of breathers/intakes  

**Acceptance:** as-received condition report; hold tags on damaged or unverified systems; photos in the asset file.  
**Stop:** structural damage, unknown fluid, uncertified rim/tire, inoperative park brake or steering at static check, fire system unserviceable if required for any later movement.  
**Owner:** Maintenance. **Reliability** owns the baseline file (this is the P-F / health starting point).  
**Do not** calculate remaining life or MTBF from a single receipt inspection.

## 6. Gate 3 — Maintenance strategy, MRO, tools (readiness, not a fake RCM)

Until OEM serial PM and site RCM/strategy exist under MOC, the maintenance posture is:

- **Preserve OEM mandatory inspections and safety-system proof tests** from the serial pack  
- **Do not** invent hour-based PM, oil-drain, or filter intervals in this framework  
- Stand up a **truck-specific job plan library** only after document control  
- Criticality: treat service brakes, retarder, steering, park brake, tires/rims, struts, hoist/body-up, fire, and operator visibility/proximity as **high-consequence** pending formal criticality (severity is not the same as causal confidence)

**Logistics / materials readiness (list from approved BOM only)**

- First-fill fluids and filters **by serial spec**  
- Wheel/rim tooling, torque tooling **as specified**, nitrogen/inflation cage or approved inflation method per **site tire standard**  
- Jacks, stands, body props, lockouts **rated for this truck** — ratings must come from approved equipment register, not this note  
- Tow hitch, recovery gear  
- Spare strut, hose, filter, sensor, and brake-related parts **only if on the approved critical-spares list**; if that list does not exist, **say so and do not guess min/max**  
- Fast-fuel nozzles, auto-lube grease type  

**Acceptance:** warehouse bin locations mapped to this serial’s BOM; “no-part, no-run” list agreed for protective functions.  
**Stop:** no approved way to jack, prop body, inflate tires, or isolate; or protective-function parts with zero coverage and no TA risk acceptance.  
**Owner:** Planning + Warehouse. **Approver:** Maintenance Superintendent.

## 7. Gate 4 — Competency (people are part of the asset)

Minimum role competencies **against site matrices** (do not invent certificate names):

| Role | Must be competent to |
|---|---|
| Operator | Isolate, park, retard, dump, wet/grade hazards, radio, payload policy **once authorized**, emergency stop/fire, no body-up travel |
| Maintainer | LOTOTO on this energy sources, strut/hose, brakes, steering accumulators, VIMS download |
| Tire/rim | Split-rim / large-tire energy — **only authorized persons** |
| Recovery | Approved tow/disable procedure for 797-class |
| Supervisor / dispatcher | Do not assign the truck until G7; know stop criteria |
| Reliability | FRACAS coding, VIMS baseline, deficiency control |

**Acceptance:** named competent persons for first-move and first-shift.  
**Stop:** no authorized operator or isolator; no tire/rim person if any wheel work is planned.  
**Wrong-call consequence:** high-energy human error. Competency sign-off is Operations + Maintenance Superintendents.

## 8. Gate 5 — Controlled commissioning (Cat 797 system lens)

Commission **this truck’s fitted systems**, not a generic mobile plant checklist. Sequence is **static/inhibited → dead-engine checks → inhibited low-energy movement → proving run under permit**. Exact tests, pressures, temperatures, and pass/fail numbers come **only** from the serial commissioning pack and site procedures.

**Functional groups to prove (presence/absence from as-built; do not tick a system that is not fitted):**

1. **Protective and isolation** — battery/master, starter interlock, park brake holding on designated grade **per procedure**, body-up interlock, hoist inhibit, emergency stops, fire detection/suppression release path, engine shutdown  
2. **Steering and hydraulics** — secondary steering (if fitted) proving, hose/clamp as-built, leaks, tank cleanliness  
3. **Service brakes and retarder** — functional proof **per OEM/site brake-test procedure**; do not invent a stopping-distance number  
4. **Powertrain** — startability, leaks, unusual noise/temp **as recorded**, shifting/lockup behavior against serial procedure  
5. **Suspension/struts** — ride height/charge **only to serial procedure**  
6. **Tires/rims/TPMS** — match, damage, inflation by tire authority  
7. **Body/hoist/dump** — body-up alarms, prop pins, dump control, tail clearance  
8. **Electrical/VIMS/telemetry/dispatch** — clock, GPS, payload if fitted, event logging, radio  
9. **Operator station** — ROPS/FOPS integrity as inspected, mirrors/cameras, HVAC, seat, controls  
10. **Fuel/auto-lube/cooling** — correct media, no cross-contamination, cooler cleanliness  
11. **Interfaces** — shovel spot, dump pocket, weighbridge, fuel bay, wash bay  

**Discriminating records (for later RCA, not for fake statistics):** first VIMS baseline, oil samples after first fill and after first proving run, thermal/leak walkdown, brake-test sheet, software version printout.

**Acceptance:** every fitted protective function has a dated pass result or an open **stop-class** deficiency.  
**Stop (examples of stop, not a complete hazard register):** any protective function fail; undocumented software; uncontrolled leak at high-energy line; tire/rim noncompliance; fire system fail; steering/brake proving fail; identity mismatch discovered mid-test.  
**Owner:** dealer commissioning lead executes; site Maintenance countersigns; **Technical Authority** accepts. **Anyone** in the isolation/HSE chain may stop.

**Lowest-regret containment if a test fails:** park in designated bermed bay, isolate, chock, body down or officially propped, hold tag, preserve VIMS and failed-part evidence. Do **not** bypass interlocks.

## 9. Gate 6 — Supervised reliability growth (not “in the fleet”)

Release only under a **written growth plan**:

- Named operators and supervisors  
- Restricted routes, payload **at or below the authorized policy** (policy must exist; if not, **do not haul production**)  
- Defined inspection cadence from serial pack + site TA (hours not invented here)  
- FRACAS: every defect gets asset ID, system, detection method, operating context, immediate containment, failed item vs suspected mechanism  
- Screen **sister 797s** only if they exist and share configuration; this request does not confirm a fleet  

**Do not** declare infant-mortality rate, Crow-AMSAA growth, or MTBF. There is no denominator.

**Acceptance to stay in G6:** no open stop-class defect; samples/logs trending under a defined review.  
**Stop / drop back to G5:** protective-function defect, repeated same mechanism, undocumented modification, or operations using the truck outside the growth envelope.  
**Owner:** Reliability (model) + Operations (envelope). **Approver:** Technical Authority.

## 10. Gate 7 — Deficiency closure and production handover

**Handover file (minimum)**

- Identity/config freeze and as-built  
- Document-control index and conflict log (closed or still quarantined with TA instruction)  
- Baseline condition + first samples + VIMS baseline  
- Commissioning signed sheets  
- Competency list for operate/maintain  
- Maintenance job plans and PM source **cited**, not invented  
- Spares/tooling readiness statement  
- Open deficiency register with classification: **stop / restrict / watch / closed**  
- Payload, speed, and route policy **as authorized** (or explicit “not authorized”)  
- Warranty/dealer contact **as contracted** (do not invent terms)  
- Named production owner after handover  

**FRACAS corrective action is not closed** at signature. It closes only after implementation **and** effectiveness over an operating period defined by TA (period not invented here) and screening of similar units if applicable.

**Acceptance:** zero stop-class items; restrict-class items have a risk owner, expiry, and operating envelope.  
**Stop:** incomplete file; disputed brake/tire/steering/payload limit; unsigned gates.  
**Approvers:** Technical Authority **and** Operations Superintendent. Reliability recommends; they authorize.

---

## 11. Gate 8 — Post-handover effectiveness (onboarding not finished at G7)

- First planned inspection completed as written  
- No silent return of G5 defects  
- Spares actually used vs BOM errors  
- Operator/maintainer feedback in FRACAS  
- Document conflicts still quarantined until MOC  

**Owner:** Reliability. **Authority to declare onboarding complete:** Technical Authority after the effectiveness window.

---

## 12. Failure thinking during onboarding (symptom vs cause)

Treat early defects as **investigation**, not as a parts-churn success.

| If you see | Failed item may be | Competing mechanisms (not yet root cause) | Discriminating evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| High brake temp / warning | Brake/retarder hardware | Overload, wrong retarding practice, haul-profile vs policy, cooling blockage, software limit, sensor fault | Payload records, route grade, VIMS, inspection, operator statement |
| Steering complaint | Pump/column/hose | Fluid type, contamination, accumulator precharge, secondary steer not proved | Fluid lab, pressure test **per OEM**, commissioning sheet |
| Strut leak / ride | Strut | Charge error, overload, haul-road, commissioning fill | Charge record, payload, road inspection |
| Tire event | Tire/rim | Inflation, mismatch, loading contact, speed, debris, manufacturing | Tire authority file — **preserve scene** |
| Overheat | Cooler/engine | Wrong coolant, blanked cooler, duty, sensor | Sample, inspection, VIMS temps |
| Fire system inhibit | Suppression | Installation incomplete, discharged, wiring | Vendor inspection |

**Do not declare verified root cause** while competing hypotheses remain open. Severity can be critical while causal confidence is low — **secure evidence first**.

## 13. Register to open now (empty until evidence exists)

Create these live registers for **this serial only**:

1. Document conflict / MOC register  
2. Deficiency / FRACAS register  
3. Protective-function proof-test register  
4. Baseline health (fluids, VIMS, software, hours)  
5. Competency authorization list  
6. Critical tooling and spare readiness (BOM-sourced)  
7. Restricted-operation envelope until G7  

All cells without site/OEM evidence stay **unsupported**.

## Bottom line

**Do not put this Cat 797 into unsupervised production.** Freeze identity and documents (**G0**), then execute G1–G8 in order using the **serial-number Cat/dealer pack and current approved site procedures**. If those conflict, **hold the last approved safe state** and escalate to document control, Technical Authority, and MOC. Crusher history is irrelevant and must not enter this asset file.

**Uncertain (blocks any numeric acceptance, PM interval, payload, or reliability metric):** exact 797 variant and BOM, serial commissioning limits, site legal/HSE applicability, duty cycle, payload policy, tire standard, shop/recovery fit, fleet sisters, and all measured baselines.

**Who may proceed:** Site Technical Authority for technical limits and gate passage; Operations Superintendent for any production assignment; HSE for statutory/isolation/traffic/fire; Maintenance Superintendent for maintain/isolate/jack; **tire/rim authorized person** for wheel work; dealer commissioning lead executes G5 but does **not** outrank site stop authority. This framework does not authorize bypass of isolations, interlocks, OEM limits, or site procedures.

**Verified facts**
- One protective bearing-temperature trip on a critical turbine.
- Historian shows a real temperature-signal spike (the recorded point moved; the event is not a missing-data artifact).
- Sensor health is unknown.
- Corroborating vibration is unknown.

**Assertions / gaps (not facts)**

**Severity versus confidence**
- **Severity (consequence if the metal was actually hot):** high. A protective bearing-temperature trip on a critical turbine is a high-consequence event: possible wipe, rotor/journal damage, oil-fire risk, and forced outage. Severity is set by asset criticality and the protective function, not by how many times it happened.
- **Confidence (that a true thermal failure occurred):** low. n = 1, measurement-chain integrity is unverified, and vibration is absent. A historian spike proves the **signal** changed, not that the **bearing** overheated. The instrument, scaling, junction, transmitter, card, or logic can be the failed item; the bearing may be the victim or uninvolved.
- High severity + low confidence means **contain and secure evidence**, not declare a root cause or defeat protection.

**Competing mechanisms (ranked, all open)**
1. Spurious / measurement-chain fault (sensor, wiring, transmitter, scaling, I/O, historian mapping).
2. True localized bearing heating (lubrication, load, alignment, clearance, oil condition) — **not confirmed**.
3. Valid trip on a short thermal transient with no lasting damage.
4. Protective-logic / setpoint / voting issue (cannot be assessed from the supplied evidence).

No mechanism is closed. Correlation in the historian is not root cause.

**Next action (lowest-regret, reversible)**
1. **Hold restart / keep the trip in force** until Technical Authority (with Operations) authorizes the next state. Do not bypass, raise, or vote-out the protective function.
2. **Preserve evidence now:** freeze trip logs, SOE, historian traces (bearing T, related T, speed, load, lube P/T/flow, alarms), as-found setpoints/voting, and work-order/FRACAS boundary (one trip, this turbine, this protective channel).

4. **Pull corroboration on the same time window:** vibration (or state why it is unavailable), lube and process conditions, other bearings, and operating-state normalization. Absence of vibration is a **coverage gap**, not proof of a healthy bearing.
5. **Discriminating tests:** loop/sensor verification and time-aligned vibration/process overlay. Physical inspection only if TA/OEM criteria are met after the signal is shown to be credible—or if other damage indicators appear.

- **This shift / next available outage window as TA directs:** I&C — measurement-chain integrity; Reliability/CM — aligned vibration and process review; Investigation owner — FRACAS problem statement and evidence pack.
